notes:
I've written verse-by-verse notes on 1 Chronicles 7 below. Most of the material comes from older commentaries on studylight.org, biblehub.com and blueletterbible.org, plus Enduring Word. Some limits first:

- **Traditions:** None of the pages I read set out Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Reformed or Lutheran positions that clash on this chapter. Where the commentators disagree, it is over how to read the text, mainly v. 21, not over doctrine.
- **Catholic and Orthodox:** I didn't find any newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org pages on this chapter. I found only the contents page of Haydock's Catholic commentary, with nothing on the verses themselves.
- **Popular modern teaching:** I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings.
- **Modern scholarship:** I found nothing from bibleodyssey.org. From the NET Bible I found only its translation, not its notes.

Two sources (the full Ellicott and Pulpit Commentary pages) came back in a form I can't cite line by line. For those points I give the page address instead.

**Chapter overview**
- Constable (Dallas Seminary): by listing 12 tribes the Chronicler emphasized that the whole nation was intact. He thinks Dan and Zebulun were left out because including them would have made 14 tribes, since Levi was counted and Manasseh's two halves were treated separately. Another possibility he mentions is that these two tribes had little influence or relevance among the Jews who made up the returned exiles. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-7.html
- Matthew Henry: He says no reason can be given, except that idolatry began among the Danites at Laish, where Jeroboam later set up a golden calf. He also notes that Dan is left out of Revelation 7. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_007.cfm

**vv. 1–5 (Issachar)**
- v. 1: Gill notes Genesis 46:13 gives the same number with two names spelled differently (Phuvah and Job), while Numbers 26:23 matches the names here. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-chronicles-7.html. The Pulpit Commentary adds that a later judge, Tola son of Puah (Judges 10:1–2), shows how family names stayed in use over long periods. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-7.html
- v. 2: Gill sees irony here: the men were famous for courage though they came from Tola, whose name means "a worm." He ties the count to Joab's census of Israel ordered by David, 1 Chronicles 21:5. (same URL). The Pulpit Commentary says that since the 22,600 figure appears nowhere else, the compiler clearly had sources we don't have. (tpc URL)
- v. 3: Clarke says only four names are listed; the Syriac and Arabic read "four," and if "five" is right, Izrahiah himself must be counted with his sons. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-chronicles-7.html
- v. 4: Gill says polygamy explains their large numbers, and they practised it to multiply Abraham's seed as God had promised. (geb URL). Enduring Word quotes Payne that 36,000 warriors from Izrahiah and four sons "seems unlikely," as does the tribal total of 145,600; this may be the first of nine passages where elep ("thousand") is better read as allup ("chief"). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-4-8/
- v. 5: The Pulpit Commentary records the debate: 87,000 fits well with the 800,000 total for all Israel (2 Samuel 24:9), though Grove adds all the figures to get 145,600, which the second census of Moses seems to count against. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-7.html. Ellicott does the sums: the rest of Issachar must have numbered 28,400 to reach 87,000. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-7.html

**vv. 6–12 (Benjamin)**
- v. 6: Clarke notes that Genesis 46:21 lists ten sons of Benjamin. He also reports that the rabbis say Ezra did not know whether some were sons or grandsons, and that his source tables were often defective. (acc URL). Gill thinks Jediael seems to be the same as Ashbel, Genesis 46:21. (geb URL)
- v. 7: Benson says these were probably not Bela's immediate sons but his grandchildren, each from a different father. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/1-chronicles-7.html. Ellicott takes the number as the fighting strength of the Belaites, who are identified with their heads. (ebc URL)
- v. 8: Gill reports Kimchi's view that the last two gave their names to Benjamite cities: Anathoth, Jeremiah's hometown, and Alameth. (geb URL)
- v. 11: Ellicott gives Benjamin's total as 54,434 against 45,600 in Moses' census. That small rise over three centuries makes sense because the tribe was nearly wiped out after the crime at Gibeah (Judges 20:47). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/7.htm. Enduring Word identifies Ehud (v. 10) as the famous leader for Israel noted in Judges 3:12-30 (EW URL). Ellicott calls him a "namesake" of the judge. (biblehub Ellicott URL)
- v. 12 (a disputed verse): Enduring Word says many read "the son of Aher" as a veiled reference to the tribe of Dan. Its reasons: Hushim is Dan's son in Genesis 46:23; v. 13 mentions Bilhah, mother of Dan and Naphtali; and otherwise Dan is missing. (EW URL). The Pulpit Commentary disagrees. It says Bertheau and Zöckler take "Aher" as "another" and link it to Dan, but the basis is "far too slender to build upon." (tpc URL). Ellicott sees no contradiction in calling Shuppim and Huppim sons of Ir: it is no different from calling one person a son of David, of Judah, and of Abraham. (biblehub Ellicott URL)

**v. 13 (Naphtali)**
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that Naphtali's land later became Galilee, which it calls the cradle of Christianity and the Lord's home. (tpc URL)

**vv. 14–19 (Manasseh)**
- v. 14: JFB suggests reading it as "Ashriel, whom his Syrian concubine bare to him, and Machir, the father of Gilead (whom his wife bare to him)." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Ch/1Ch_007.cfm. Ellicott argues the bracketed comment is there to warn the reader that Asriel was the "son" of the Aramean concubine only indirectly, through descent from Machir. (biblehub Ellicott URL)
- v. 15: Ellicott suggests a few words have dropped out that named Machir's second wife and Zelophehad's descent from her. He also thinks the passage points to Aramean and Benjamite elements in Western Manasseh. (same URL). The Pulpit Commentary points readers to the story of Zelophehad's daughters in Numbers 27 and 36. Its homiletic section praises Moses' ruling that daughters may inherit where there are no sons, calling it a wise adjustment of law to new cases. (tpc URL)
- v. 17: Ellicott says Bedan here is a clan, not a person. (biblehub Ellicott URL). The Pulpit Commentary thinks he may be the Bedan of 1 Samuel 12:11. (tpc URL)
- v. 18: Gill notes that the Vulgate translates Hammolecheth as "a queen," and that Gideon's family came from Abiezer. (geb URL)

**vv. 20–29 (Ephraim)**
- v. 21 (the main disputed verse: who raided whom?):
  - *The Ephraimites were the raiders, while still in Egypt.* JFB says the episode seems to have happened before Israel left Egypt, while the patriarch Ephraim was alive. A raid would fit the habits of Oriental shepherds. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Ch/1Ch_007.cfm
  - *The men of Gath were the raiders.* JFB offers this alternative as well, reading "when" instead of "because." On that reading the men of Gath attacked the Ephraimite flocks and killed the shepherds. (same URL). Matthew Henry prefers this reading because the Israelites in Egypt were shepherds, not soldiers https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_007.cfm. Gill also argues that "came down" describes travel from Palestine to Egypt, not from Egypt to Palestine. (geb URL)
  - *The raid happened after the settlement in Canaan.* Ellicott: the raid was made on Philistia from the hill country of Ephraim, early in the tribe's settlement in Canaan. (ebc URL)
  - *Keil & Delitzsch* take the Ephraimites as the cattle-raiders. But they ask how Ephraim could have another son afterwards, since he died long before the Exodus. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-chronicles-7.html
  - *The Pulpit Commentary* calls the passage having very little collateral evidence and says it is no impossibility. (tpc URL)
  - *A lesson drawn by Henry:* Some think the Ephraimites jumped ahead of God's timing. Henry's lesson: "Those that will not wait God's time cannot expect God's blessing." (mhc URL)
- vv. 22–23: Ellicott offers two readings. Either the passage is a metaphorical description of the tribe's weakening and later recovery through a new clan, Beriah, or it is literal. He also notes a wordplay: Beriah ("gift") sounds like the Hebrew for "in evil." (ebc URL). Benson (Methodist): when God restores comfort to mourners, we should set the mercies against the crosses. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/1-chronicles-7.html. The Pulpit Commentary links the relatives' visit to Eastern custom (see Job 2:11; John 11:19). (tpc URL). The Preacher's Homiletical commentary compares Beriah to Seth, another seed instead of Abel, whom Cain slew. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/1-chronicles-7.html. Wesley's notes on Numbers 1 say the devil in vain attempted to defeat Ephraim's promised growth through the men of Gath. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/numbers-1.html
- v. 24: Ellicott says "daughter" must mean simply a female descendant, since a literal daughter of Ephraim or Beriah could not have founded these places. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/7-24.htm. Clarke cites the Targum: her name means "remnant," because she survived the slaughter. (acc URL). The Pulpit Commentary's homiletics hold her up as a woman worthy of being held in lasting remembrance. (tpc URL)
- vv. 25–27: Gill traces the line through Elishama, prince of Ephraim in the wilderness (Numbers 1:10), down to Joshua. (geb URL). The Pulpit Commentary calls the chronology unresolvable and the passage "mutilated and corrupt," though very old. (tpc URL). On Joshua, the Pulpit homiletics say it is better the humblest post among Jesus' followers than the proudest place in Joshua's ranks. (tpc URL)
- v. 28: Gill says the town is not the Philistine Gaza; the Targum calls it Aiah. (geb URL)
- v. 29: Ellicott: these towns lay in Issachar and Asher but were given to Manasseh. They mark the northern edge of Joseph's tribes, as v. 28 marks the southern. (ebc URL)

**vv. 30–40 (Asher)**
- vv. 30–32: Enduring Word quotes Clarke reporting the rabbis' claim that Asher's daughters were very beautiful and all married kings or priests. (EW URL). Ellicott says Birzaith may mean "well of olive." (ebc URL)
- v. 34: The Pulpit Commentary says "Ahi" might mean "his brother," i.e. Shomer's brother (more literally "and his brother"). (tpc URL)
- v. 39: Ellicott notes that Ulla does not seem connected with the foregoing genealogy. https://biblehub.com/1_chronicles/7-39.htm
- v. 40: Keil & Delitzsch explain the lower number: 26,000 counts only men able to fight from one family, Heber's, the only one whose register survived. (kdo URL). Ellicott suggests that if this is David's census, the tribe may have declined by his day. (ebc URL). The Pulpit Commentary notes that Asher, like Simeon, gave no judge to the nation. It also points to Anna of the tribe of Asher (Luke 2:36). (tpc URL)
